name: Titanium step plate genioplasty fixation

card.summary: The titanium step-shaped plate and screws used to hold a repositioned chin bone in place after sliding genioplasty, locking in the new chin projection.
card.note: Part of a surgical procedure with nerve, infection and soft-tissue risks.

quick.overview:
In sliding genioplasty, a section of the chin bone is cut and moved forward, backward or vertically. The titanium step plate is a small stair-shaped plate screwed across the cut to hold the segment in its new position while it heals, so the chin keeps the projection the surgeon created.

The approach is the usual fixation method for the procedure, with wires and jaw wiring as an alternative. A 2021 plastic surgery study compared it with a no-degloving lag-screw approach.
quick.how: Surgeons attach the step plate to the moved chin segment and the lower jaw with screws, usually through an incision inside the mouth. Recovery involves soft foods and reduced chewing at first.
quick.risks: Genioplasty risks include swelling, bruising, temporary lip numbness or weakness, infection and nerve damage. A soft-tissue droop called witch's chin can occur, linked in one study to excess soft-tissue degloving.

lead: A titanium step plate is the fixation hardware commonly used in sliding genioplasty. After a horseshoe-shaped piece of the chin bone is cut and moved forward or backward, the plate and screws hold it in the new position [1]. The goal is a chin whose projection and balance match the rest of the face.
Wikipedia lists titanium step plates and screws as the usual way to fix the repositioned bone, with fine wires and about three to four weeks of intermaxillary fixation as an alternative [1].
A 2021 comparison of 50 patients found that a traditional stair-step plate technique with degloving and a no-degloving lag-screw method had similar advancement and complication rates [2].

chain: Chin bone is cut and slid to a new position
Step plate and screws hold it
Healed chin keeps the intended projection
angle.text: The plate stabilises the moved bone so the surgical change in chin projection or length becomes permanent as the bone heals.

paras: Sliding genioplasty moves a horseshoe-shaped chin segment forward to increase projection or backward to reduce it [1]. The step shape lets the plate sit across the cut with one portion on each side of the offset, which suits a segment that has been advanced.

In the 2021 study, the traditional group used degloving to place a stair-step plate; the no-degloving group used lag-screw fixation. Horizontal and vertical changes were about 5 mm and 2 mm versus 6 mm and 2 mm, operating time and complication rate (5 percent) were similar, and the study focused on reducing chin ptosis, or witch's chin [2].

Step plates are used elsewhere in surgery; one cadaveric study found a locked step-plate withstood more force than a single screw for a calcaneal osteotomy [3], and a retrospective study of 90 cleft patients reported step-plate stabilisation in Le Fort I advancement [4].
A 2021 comparison of 25 patients per group evaluated stair-step plate and lag-screw genioplasty [2]. Other step-plate studies concern different bones [3][4].

Genioplasty commonly causes swelling, bruising and temporary lower-lip numbness or weakness; less commonly infection, bony change, displacement and nerve damage [1]. Witch's chin is thought to come from excessive soft-tissue degloving without reattaching the mentalis muscle [2].
